deep.reconstruction:
Context: the previous page computes the Mellin transform of the theta-type series 2K/π − 1, giving π^{-s}Π(s−1)(1−2^{-s})ζ(s)L(s,χ₋₄). The next page studies saddle points of e^{nx}x^{s−1}/(e^x−1). This page evaluates the basic 'Mordell-type' integral that underlies Riemann's integral representation of ζ(s), the one Siegel later extracted from the Nachlass.

(1) Object. The first line is ∫ e^{x²/(4πi)+βx}/(1−e^x) dx. The exponent may first have been written x²/(2πi), and the denominator is overwritten.

(2) Termwise idea. Expanding 1/(1−e^x)=Σ_{n≥0} e^{nx} gives terms e^{x²/(4πi)+(β+n)x}. Riemann completes the square:
x²/(4πi)+(β+n)x = (1/(4πi))(x+2πi(β+n))² − πi(β+n)².
Riemann writes only '−πi nn'. Each term would then be a Fresnel/Gaussian integral times e^{−πi(β+n)²}. This approach is abandoned in favour of a contour shift.

(3) Definition. Q = Q(β) = ∫_{−∞}^{∞} e^{x²/(4πi)+βx}/(e^x−1) dx. For convergence, the path must be a line of slope −1, i.e. direction e^{−iπ/4} (for example x = c·i + r e^{−iπ/4} with 0<c<2π), so that it avoids the poles 2πik. This specification is mine.

(4) Substitution x = y+2πi. Then x²/(4πi) = y²/(4πi) + y + πi and βx = βy + 2πiβ, while e^x = e^y. Hence the integral over the shifted line equals e^{πi+2βπi} ∫ e^{y²/(4πi)+y+βy}/(e^y−1) dy. This matches the manuscript.

(5) Completion (implicit; mine). Write e^y/(e^y−1) = 1 + 1/(e^y−1). Then Q(β+1) = Q(β) + G(β), where
G(β) = ∫ e^{x²/(4πi)+βx} dx = 2π e^{−πi/4} e^{−πiβ²}.
The strip between L and L+2πi contains exactly one pole, x=2πi. Its residue is e^{(2πi)²/(4πi)+2πiβ} = −e^{2πiβ}. Therefore
Q − (−e^{2πiβ})(Q+G) = 2πi(−e^{2πiβ}).
Multiplying by e^{−2πiβ} gives
Q(e^{−2βπi}+1) = −2πi − 2π e^{−πi/4} e^{−πiβ²},
which is the expression the page breaks off at. So
Q(β) = −2π(i + e^{−πi/4}e^{−πiβ²})/(1+e^{−2πiβ}).
Sanity check: at β=1/2 both numerator and denominator vanish, so the singularity is removable.

This closed evaluation is equivalent, after the scaling x→2πix, to Riemann's formula ∫_{0↙1} e^{−πix²+2πiux}/(e^{πix}−e^{−πix}) dx = (e^{πiu²}−… )/(…), as reported by Siegel. Riemann uses that formula to obtain the Riemann–Siegel integral representation of ζ(s).
errors: Completing the square: the constant should be −πi(β+n)², not −πi n². This is a slip, or a shorthand with β suppressed.

No contour or path is specified. On the real axis the integral does not converge (oscillatory Gaussian times e^{βx}), and it would pass through the pole x=0. A line in direction e^{−iπ/4} avoiding the poles is required. This is implicit, not an error of substance.
The derivation stops at the left side Q(e^{−2βπi}+1); the right side (−2πi minus the Gaussian term) is not written on this page.
Minor inconsistency: the first line has denominator 1−e^x and possibly x²/(2πi), while Q uses e^x−1 and x²/(4πi).

results.what: Closed-form evaluation of ∫ e^{x²/(4πi)+βx}/(e^x−1) dx by shifting the contour by 2πi, using the residue at 2πi and a Gaussian (Fresnel) integral, giving a linear equation for Q
results.modern_name: Evaluation of the Mordell integral at the special parameter (Riemann's lemma for the Riemann–Siegel integral formula)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (Nachlass), published by C. L. Siegel 1932; general Mordell integrals by Mordell 1933

results.what: Completing the square in x²/(4πi)+(β+n)x after the geometric expansion of 1/(1−e^x)
results.modern_name: Gaussian/Fresnel integral by completing the square

deep.surprise_reason: This is the known Nachlass computation underlying the Riemann–Siegel integral formula. Siegel (1932) explicitly published and credited Riemann's evaluation of this integral, so the page is a working draft of an already-attributed result.
